title: Credit Spreads and Business Cycle Fluctuations
datasets: Federal Reserve H.15 Selected Interest Rates
research_question: Do bond-level, duration-matched corporate credit spreads forecast future US real activity beyond the term spread and policy rate, and does that forecasting power reflect default risk or a separate, time-varying excess bond premium tied to financial-intermediary risk-bearing capacity?
main_finding: The GZ credit spread substantially outperforms the Baa-Aaa and paper-bill spreads as a predictor of employment, industrial production and GDP growth; most of this predictive power, especially after 1985, comes from the excess bond premium rather than measured default risk, and orthogonalized shocks to the premium produce sizeable, persistent declines in consumption, investment, output and equity prices in a VAR.
research_gaps: Sample restricted to large, bond-market-active firms; bank-dependent firms untested
Causal, credit-supply interpretation of excess-bond-premium shocks relies on a standard but unverified recursive VAR ordering
No out-of-sample / real-time forecast evaluation is reported
Cannot cleanly separate the risk-bearing-capacity channel from a time-varying disaster-risk alternative
research_ideas: Construct an excess bank-loan premium from syndicated loan pricing data to test the mechanism among bank-dependent firms
Extend the excess bond premium to a growth-at-risk, quantile-regression framework
High-frequency identification of excess-bond-premium shocks around bank-capital and regulatory announcements
Construct a euro-area analogue of the GZ spread to test the mechanism against the sovereign-bank nexus
Use option-implied disaster-risk measures to separate the risk-bearing-capacity channel from time-varying disaster risk

title: Credit Cycles
subfield: Macro-Finance / Collateral Constraints and Business Cycles
datasets: None (theoretical paper; illustrative numerical simulation only)
research_question: In an economy where debt must be secured by durable, productive collateral, how large and how persistent are the responses of asset prices, investment and output to a small, temporary shock, and can the interaction between debt and collateral generate cycles on its own?
main_finding: Because the collateral asset's price capitalizes the entire expected future path of credit-constraint tightness, the dynamic multiplier on asset prices exceeds the static multiplier by a factor equal to the inverse of the net real interest rate; a temporary 1% shock generates land-price and output responses of comparable size to the shock, persisting roughly a decade, and lumpy investment can generate damped, multi-year predator-prey cycles between debt and landholding.
research_gaps: No priced credit risk: lenders are risk-neutral, so the model speaks to credit quantities, not credit spreads
No theory of who becomes credit-constrained or when
Mechanism not robust to hedging markets against the aggregate shock (Krishnamurthy 2003)
Purely deterministic, one-time shock; authors flag a fully stochastic extension as the 'pressing next step'
research_ideas: Solve a fully stochastic, globally-solved version of the model with recurring, anticipated shocks
Test the lumpy-investment build-up prediction against farm- or firm-level micro data
Endogenize the supply of hedging instruments to restore amplification and generate a priced credit spread
Cross-country test of the elasticity threshold separating cyclical from monotonic collateral dynamics
Horse race between collateral-constraint and heterogeneous-beliefs explanations of asset-price overshooting
